newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus cuts rates on way to deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus cuts rates on way to deregulation.

text.p: The Central Bank of Cyprus said on Thursday it would cut its lending rate to commercial banks to 7.0 percent from 7.5 percent, effective Friday January 17.
The cut was widely seen as the first step towards deregulation of interest rates, now set by law at a maximum nine percent.
The government wants them deregulated before the island starts accession talks with the European Union in roughly 12 months' time.
Central Bank Governor Afxentis Afxentiou said that the bank would also cut its overnight deposit rate to 4.0 percent from 5.0 percent, effective January 17.
The governor told reporters the central bank expects commercial banks to follow suit with reductions in their retail rates, now 8.5 percent for loans and 7.0 percent for deposits.
"We shall look at whether a (central bank) intervention is required," Afxentiou said, referring to the possibility of the central bank telling commercial banks to lower their rates.
He said the matter would also be discussed with co-operatives, which are currently not subject to central bank instructions.
Interest rates were last reduced by commercial banks in two stages in 1994, with a 50-basis point cut in the deposit rate followed months later with a 50-basis point cut in lending rates.

The latest cut is expected to reinvigorate business activity, which has recently shown a slowdown and to absorb excess liquidity in the banking system which has accumulated due to low demand, central bank officials said. It is also expected to spur investor interest in the Cyprus stock exchange.

Deputies in parliament are due to resume a debate on Thursday afternoon into the government's intention to scrap the interest rate ceiling. Communist Akel, the second largest party with 19 seats in the 56-member house, opposes deregulation because of fearss it could drive rates up.
